newsitem.title: USA: S.F. Fed's Parry optimistic on growth, inflation.
newsitem.headline: S.F. Fed's Parry optimistic on growth, inflation.

text.p: Robert Parry, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of San Francisco, expressed optimism on Monday about the outlook for growth and inflation in 1997, saying the economy is on a solid footing and that prices appear surprisingly well behaved.
In an interview, Parry said the nearly over 1996 was shaping up to be a "pretty good year."
"For 1997, it would seem to me that one can be reasonably optimistic," he added.

On a fourth-quarter-to-fourth quarter basis, Parry predicted that U.S. gross domestic product growth would come in at around 2.6 percent in 1996 "or something like that, depending on what happens in the fourth quarter."
The U.S. Commerce Department has estimated that growth came in at 2.2 percent in the third quarter after a 4.7 percent burst of strength in the second quarter.
"It looks like we've slowed to a more sustainable rate," Parry said, saying the cooling down of the economy had helped to ease concerns about inflation.

The San Francisco Fed chief said he looked for inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index to come in at around 3.0 percent in 1996, which he said was a bit on the high side due to jumps in food and energy prices earlier this year.
However, he expected the closely watched "core" CPI rate, excluding food and energy, would be a relatively benign 2.6 percent.
Overall, he said, "Inflation has been quite good."
Parry added that inflation has performed surprisingly well in light of capacity constraints such as a low unemployment rate that in past periods had caused inflation to rise.
The U.S. unemployment rate is now at 5.2 percent, below the 5.5 to 6.0 percent range that some economists say constitutes effective full employment.

Parry, who predicted the economy would expand at about a trend rate of 2.0 percent in 1997 and that unemployment would hover around current levels, said recent price developments have made him more optimistic about inflation in the coming year.
Given a continued low jobless rate, the possibility exists for inflation to trend higher, said Parry, who added that a "caution light" was still appropriate.
However, he added, "I am less convinced that will happen given how well inflation has performed."
Parry was not a voting member of the Fed's policy-setting Federal Open Market Committee this year but he will vote in 1997.

In part because of a more favorable outlook for inflation, market interest rates in the United States have declined from levels upwards of 7 percent in the summer. The benchmark 30- year U.S. Treasury bond stood at 6.42 in afternoon trade Monday.
Asked whether such levels might be overly stimulative to the economy after the cooling down in growth experienced in recent months, Parry replied he did not think so.
"The kind of moves we're seeing (in bond prices) are not big moves," he said, saying that the recent rates were "not all that stimulative."

Concerning the condition of the Twelfth Federal Reserve District, which includes California, Oregon, Nevada, Idaho, Arizona, Utah, Alaska and Hawaii, Parry said the region's economy looked very strong.
Noting that the area is close to a fifth of the national economy, he said its health contributed to an upbeat outlook for the U.S. economy as a whole.
